name: Donegal
tagline: Ireland's wild, sparsely visited far northwest, home to Europe's highest sea cliffs and some of the country's emptiest coastline.
highlight: Standing at the top of Slieve League as the cliffs drop 600 metres straight to the Atlantic, with barely another visitor in sight.
shortDescription: Ireland's remote northwestern county, home to Slieve League's towering sea cliffs, Glenveagh National Park and some of the country's least-visited coastline.
metaDescription: A Donegal travel guide: Slieve League, Glenveagh National Park, Malin Head, food and how to plan a visit to Ireland's wild, remote northwest.
nearestAirport: Donegal Airport (CFN), or Ireland West Airport Knock (NOC)
knownFor: Slieve League's sea cliffs, Glenveagh National Park, empty coastline
goodFor: Remote hiking, dramatic coastline, real solitude

image.file: File:A sea stack in the bay at Slieve League sea cliffs.jpg
image.alt: The sea cliffs of Slieve League in County Donegal

intro: Donegal is Ireland's wild northwestern edge, a county of sea cliffs, empty beaches and mountains that sees a fraction of the visitors drawn to the southwest's Ring of Kerry or Dingle.
Its centrepiece is Slieve League, among the highest sea cliffs in Europe at nearly 600 metres, reached by a road and trail with barely a fraction of the Cliffs of Moher's crowds.
Most visitors combine a couple of days here with Glenveagh National Park's mountains and lakes further north, rewarding those willing to travel further off Ireland's classic first-timer route.

whyVisit.intro: Donegal's case rests on dramatic natural scenery with a fraction of the visitors seen elsewhere in Ireland.

points.title: Slieve League is taller than the Cliffs of Moher
points.text: Among the highest sea cliffs in Europe, at nearly three times the height, with far fewer visitors.

points.title: Glenveagh National Park is one of Ireland's wildest
points.text: A remote valley of lakes and mountains, home to a genuine reintroduced golden eagle population.

points.title: Malin Head is Ireland's most northerly point
points.text: A dramatic, windswept headland with real end-of-the-world character.

points.title: The coastline here is emptier than the southwest
points.text: Long stretches of beach and cliff with real solitude, even in peak summer.

points.title: It rewards visitors willing to travel further
points.text: A real sense of discovery for those who make the trip north.

attractionsIntro: Donegal's essential sights are spread across a large, sparsely populated county best explored by car.

attractions.name: Slieve League Cliffs

image.file: File:Slieve League Cliffs, County Donegal, Ireland6.jpg
image.alt: The towering sea cliffs of Slieve League in County Donegal

attractions.text: Among the highest sea cliffs in Europe, rising nearly 600 metres straight from the Atlantic, with a fraction of the Cliffs of Moher's crowds.
attractions.tip: Park at Bunglass viewpoint for the best views without a long hike.

attractions.name: Donegal Castle

image.alt: Donegal Castle in Donegal town

attractions.text: A well-restored 15th-century Gaelic chieftain's castle right in Donegal town, combining Irish and later Jacobean architecture.
attractions.tip: The guided tour is worth the extra time for the castle's layered history.

attractions.name: Glenveagh National Park

image.alt: Lough Beagh in Glenveagh National Park, County Donegal

attractions.text: A remote, wild valley of lakes and mountains, one of Ireland's largest national parks and home to a reintroduced golden eagle population.
attractions.tip: The shuttle bus from the visitor centre to the castle saves a long walk in.

attractions.name: Glenveagh Castle

image.alt: Glenveagh Castle beside Lough Beagh in County Donegal

attractions.text: A romantic 19th-century castle on the shore of Lough Beagh, with elaborate gardens sheltered within the wild valley.
attractions.tip: The walled garden is a surprising, sheltered contrast to the open mountains around it.

attractions.name: Malin Head

image.alt: Malin Head, the most northerly point in Ireland

attractions.text: Ireland's most northerly point, a dramatic, windswept headland with real end-of-the-world character.
attractions.tip: Look for Banba's Crown, the old signal tower at the headland's tip.

attractions.name: Fanad Head Lighthouse

image.alt: Fanad Head Lighthouse on the Donegal coast

attractions.text: Regarded as one of the world's most beautiful lighthouses, perched dramatically above Lough Swilly's entrance.
attractions.tip: Book ahead to stay overnight in the lighthouse keeper's cottages for a truly remote experience.

attractions.name: Glencolmcille

image.alt: The remote valley of Glencolmcille in County Donegal

attractions.text: A remote Irish-speaking valley, home to a folk village museum recreating centuries of rural Donegal life.
attractions.tip: One of the further-flung stops in the county, rewarding those who make the drive out.

thingsToDoIntro: Donegal rewards slower, more independent travel than the busier southwest.

thingsToDo.title: Hike Slieve League's cliff path

image.alt: The cliff-edge hiking path at Slieve League

thingsToDo.text: A rewarding, if exposed, trail beyond the Bunglass car park toward the cliffs' higher sections.
thingsToDo.tip: Stay well back from the edge — the path narrows considerably beyond the main viewpoint.

thingsToDo.title: Explore Donegal Castle

image.alt: The interior of Donegal Castle

thingsToDo.text: A worthwhile hour in Donegal town, exploring the restored castle's Gaelic and Jacobean history.
thingsToDo.tip: Combine with a wander around Donegal town's compact centre and Diamond square.

thingsToDo.title: Walk Glenveagh's castle gardens

image.alt: The gardens at Glenveagh Castle in County Donegal

thingsToDo.text: A sheltered, cultivated contrast to the wild valley around it, walled gardens set against open mountains.
thingsToDo.tip: Combine with a longer lakeside walk if time allows.

thingsToDo.title: Stand at Ireland's most northerly point

image.alt: The dramatic headland at Malin Head, Ireland's most northerly point

thingsToDo.text: A bucket-list stop for many Irish road-trippers, standing at the true northern tip of the island.
thingsToDo.tip: Bring a proper windproof layer — Malin Head lives up to its exposed reputation.

thingsToDo.title: Visit Fanad Head Lighthouse

image.alt: Fanad Head Lighthouse overlooking Lough Swilly

thingsToDo.text: A dramatic, photogenic stop, with guided tours of the lighthouse itself available in season.
thingsToDo.tip: The surrounding coast road offers some of Donegal's best, least-visited coastal views.

thingsToDo.title: Learn traditional life at Glencolmcille Folk Village

image.file: File:Cottages at Glencolmcille Folk Village Museum - geograph.org.uk - 7529909.jpg
image.alt: Traditional thatched cottages at Glencolmcille Folk Village Museum

thingsToDo.text: An engaging open-air museum of recreated cottages, tracing rural Donegal life across three centuries.
thingsToDo.tip: Combine with the valley's own craft shops, including a working weaver's cottage.

accommodation.intro: Donegal town serves as the county's main base, with smaller guesthouses scattered across the wider region.

areas.name: Donegal town
areas.bestFor: Being central and well-equipped for a first stop
areas.text: The most practical base, with the widest choice of guesthouses and restaurants.

areas.name: Near Glencolmcille or Slieve League
areas.text: Small guesthouses closer to the cliffs and the far southwestern coast, for a slower pace.

gettingThere.intro: Donegal requires more travel time than the southwest, given its remote northwestern position.

options.mode: Rental car from Dublin or Galway
options.text: The most practical way in, though a real time commitment given the distance.
options.detail: About three and a half hours from Dublin, or two and a half from Galway.

options.text: A scenic small regional airport with limited routes, mainly to Dublin.
options.detail: Widely considered one of the world's most scenic runways, landing beside the Atlantic.

options.text: A workable, if slow, option from Dublin, Galway and other major towns.
options.detail: A practical budget alternative given limited flight and no direct train options.

gettingAround.intro: A car is essential for exploring Donegal's spread-out, sparsely populated landscape.

options.text: Essential for reaching Slieve League, Glenveagh and Malin Head at a flexible pace.
options.detail: Distances here are longer than in the more compact southwest.

options.text: Easy — the town itself is small and walkable.
options.detail: Wider county sights all require a car or organised tour.

options.text: Limited compared to the southwest, given lower visitor numbers.
options.detail: Worth booking ahead if travelling without your own car.

bestTime.headline: May, June and September for the clearest views and mildest weather
bestTime.summary: Donegal is visitable year-round, though its exposed cliffs and headlands are far more pleasant outside winter storms.

seasons.text: Good odds of clear visibility at Slieve League and Malin Head.
The warmest season, though still far quieter than the southwest's peak crowds.
A quiet, often mild window with good weather odds.
Dramatic but often severe, with real risk of exposed cliff paths closing in storms.

bestTime.avoid: Exposed coastal walks at Slieve League or Malin Head in high wind — a serious hazard on Donegal's most dramatic stretches.

days.summary: The Slieve League cliffs and Donegal Castle.

days.afternoon: Donegal Castle and the town centre.

days.title: Glenveagh and the far north
days.summary: Glenveagh National Park and Malin Head or Fanad Head.
days.morning: Glenveagh National Park and Glenveagh Castle.

days.evening: Return to Donegal town or overnight further north.

tipsIntro: Practical notes that make a Donegal visit noticeably smoother.
tips: Budget more driving time than expected — Donegal's distances are longer than the southwest's.
Check wind conditions before any cliff-edge walk at Slieve League or Malin Head.
Fill up on fuel before heading into remote parts of the county — stations are sparse.
Book Fanad Head Lighthouse tours or overnight stays well ahead.
Pack a proper windproof layer regardless of season — Donegal's coast is exposed.
Allow extra time versus the map distance — rural roads here are slow, much like elsewhere in Ireland.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Donegal?
faq.a: Two days covers Slieve League, Donegal town and Glenveagh National Park comfortably; more time allows a trip to Malin Head or Fanad Head.

faq.q: Is Slieve League better than the Cliffs of Moher?
faq.a: Different rather than better — Slieve League is taller and far less crowded, though its viewpoints and facilities are more basic than the Cliffs of Moher's visitor centre.

faq.q: Is Donegal worth the extra travel time?
faq.a: Yes, for visitors with time for a longer trip — its scenery rivals the southwest with a fraction of the visitors.
Its dramatic, sparsely visited coastline, including Slieve League's cliffs and Malin Head, Ireland's most northerly point.

faq.q: Do you need a car in Donegal?
faq.a: Yes, essential — the county's sights are spread across a large, sparsely populated area with limited public transport.

faq.q: Is Glenveagh National Park worth visiting?
faq.a: Yes — it's one of Ireland's wildest national parks, with a romantic castle and real chances to spot golden eagles.
